t7hu-patterns: Heads-Up Is the Battlefield of Reading People

Heads-up faces one opponent, so reading people is amplified enormously — you don't juggle multiple table images, just this one player. HU player tendencies usually classify into a few types: Calling Station (almost never folds postflop), nit/tight-passive (very narrow range, folds too much), Maniac (aggressive and loose), TAG (balanced but predictable). After identifying the type, your exploitation strategy has direction.

Reading people isn't guessing hands — it's estimating ranges. "Calls too much" means his range skews wide and weak; "folds too much" means his range is very narrow and stealable. Inferring ranges from frequencies is the core of pattern recognition.
From Frequency to Range: Four Key Dimensions

Watch four frequencies of a HU opponent: (1) preflop open rate — how wide he plays; (2) fold rate vs C-Bets — whether he over-folds; (3) 3-bet rate — his aggression; (4) showdown tendency — calling station or controlled. Cross these four frequencies and you get a fairly complete portrait. Sample at least 50-100 hands; single-hand impressions don't count.

Example: A HU opponent opens 85% preflop (wide) but folds to C-Bets 60% (over-folds). Portrait: wide open + many folds = "wide range + weak defense". Exploitation direction: as the side acting last, C-Bet at high frequency to steal because his fold rate is high; and his wide open means your defense from the BB can also widen. Harvest two leaks at once.

Example 2 (calling station): The opponent almost never folds postflop (fold rate <25%) but opens moderately. Portrait: calling station. Exploitation: don't use pure bluffs (he doesn't fold); switch to value-bet thin value — top pair weak kicker can also bet for money because he calls with worse. Meanwhile reduce bluff frequency, converting bluffs to semi-bluffs or checks.

Example 3 (nit): The opponent opens only 30% and folds too much to raises. Portrait: nit. Exploitation: raise steal and raise frequency (his fold rate is automatic profit); but beware his occasional strong-hand re-raise — when a nit enters a pot he's usually strong.

Counterintuitive point: don't reclassify an opponent because he "once" showed the nuts. Heads-up is high-frequency; a single all-in win/loss is noise; only 50-100 hand frequency statistics form an exploitable signal. Concluding from a single-hand impression is exploitation's biggest enemy.

Build an opponent notebook: every 20 hands record the four frequencies (open rate / fold rate / 3-bet rate / showdown tendency). Among HU pros, "note-taking while playing" is the discipline that turns short-term impressions into long-term advantage.

The stat shapes of four heads-up opponent types and the matching adjustments: the same numbers in different combinations point to completely different exploits — read the shape first, then talk about magnitude.
t7hu-exploit: Exploitation Isn't Abandoning GTO — It's Calibrating It

Exploitative strategy profits from the opponent's deviations from equilibrium. But HU pros don't "abandon" GTO; they "calibrate" it: using equilibrium frequencies as the baseline and making minimum necessary deviations against the opponent's clear deviations. The key discipline — every deviation opens your own leaks, so the magnitude must be controlled and you must return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

The right posture of exploitation: aim the direction at the opponent's leak (Maximally Exploitative), keep the magnitude minimal (Minimally Exploitative). The goal of deviating is "earn enough before he corrects", not "turn yourself into a leak too".
Node Locking: Turning Exploitation Into Calculation

Node locking is an advanced solver feature: lock the opponent's strategy at a node to the real tendency you observed (e.g. "this opponent never bluffs the river" or "folds to C-Bets 60%"), then re-solve your optimal response. The output is the maximally exploitative strategy against that leak. This turns exploitation from "feel" into "calculation".

Raising steals against an over-folding opponent (SB min-raise to 2BB, BB fold rate f):

EV(steal) = f×1.5 − (1−f)×1.5

Equilibrium fold rate about 40% (f=0.4) → EV = 0.4×1.5 − 0.6×1.5 = −0.3BB (unprofitable, needs postflop recovery)

If the opponent folds 60% (f=0.6) → EV = 0.6×1.5 − 0.4×1.5 = +0.3BB (pure steal already profits)

Conclusion: for every 10% the opponent's fold rate rises, your steal frequency should rise too — but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 50%". (Concept from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.13 exploitative betting and frequencies)

Example: After locking "BB folds to turn double-barrel 55% (equilibrium ~45%)" and re-solving, the solver immediately pushes your turn bluff frequency higher, even adding weak hands that originally checked into the betting range. It precisely shows "how much you should deviate for every 1% the opponent deviates" to harvest. Node locking turns exploitation from intuition into calculation.

Example 2 (value vs the calling station): The opponent calls too loosely postflop (station). After locking this tendency, your value-bet sizes can increase and thin-value hands (top pair weak kicker) all enter the betting range — because the station calls with weak hands, your wide value range gets overpaid.

Example 3 (when to return to baseline): After you raise steal frequency, the opponent starts 3-betting frequently in response — he's discovered your deviation. Now you must return to the GTO baseline (narrow the steal range, reduce pure bluffs), or your newly opened leaks get harvested in reverse. Exploitation is a dynamic game: deviate → get detected → return to baseline, looping.

Counterintuitive point: the biggest risk of exploitation isn't "exploiting too little" but "over-exploiting and becoming the leak yourself". While harvesting the opponent's leaks, HU pros always keep one hand on the GTO baseline wheel — the moment the opponent adjusts, they snap back.

Exploitation execution in five steps: (1) HUD-collect enough samples to confirm the leak; (2) lock the node in a solver for the optimal response; (3) compare to baseline and mark the pushed-up frequencies and sizes; (4) execute live; (5) re-check the sample every 500 hands. A "lock" without data support is exploitation on paper.

Reading steal expectation off the fold rate (0.5 dead blind already sunk, raise to 2BB, the 1.5-to-1.5 model): EV = f x 1.5 - (1 - f) x 1.5. Every step up in the fold rate lifts the pure-steal expectation linearly, and 50% is break-even.
t7hu-stats: Stats Are the Skeleton of a Profile

Stats do not tell you which two cards the opponent holds; they tell you which slice of ranges he puts money in with, and where he gives up. Heads-up is played almost every hand in wide blind-versus-blind ranges, so the baselines shift up: the opening side's range sits near or above half of hands, the defending side wider still. Read heads-up with full-ring baselines and everyone looks like a maniac.

Three definitions (same hand sample):

VPIP = hands with voluntary money in / total hands
PFR = preflop raises / total hands
AF = (bets + raises) / calls

150-hand sample: 35 VPIP hands, 28 preflop raises, 60 bets / 30 raises / 30 calls
VPIP = 35 / 150 = 23.3%
PFR = 28 / 150 = 18.7%
AF = (60 + 30) / 30 = 3.0

Worked hand (the gap reads passivity): VPIP 23.3% and PFR 18.7% differ by 4.6 points, and that gap is the slice of hands he plays without raising. Rearrange the same numbers — VPIP 23.3%, PFR 23.0% — and the profile changes completely: the first is passive, the second a polarised tight-aggressive player.
FCB and WWSF: Two Conversion Rates on the Heads-Up Side

FCB is the fold rate against a continuation bet, which measures how easily one barrel takes the pot away; WWSF is the share of pots won after seeing a flop, which measures how well he converts postflop involvement into pots. In heads-up the two are more tightly linked than in full ring: with no multiway dilution, one player giving up is another collecting. Both typically sit in the forties to fifties (empirical range, not a precise promise).

Sample noise (binomial standard error and the 95% interval):

SE = sqrt(p(1-p) / n), 95% half-width = 1.96 x SE

p = 0.45:
n = 100 -> SE = 5.0 points, half-width = +/-9.8 points
n = 300 -> SE = 2.9 points, half-width = +/-5.6 points

To pull the half-width down to 2.5 points (the minimum for telling 5-point differences apart):
n >= 1.96^2 x 0.45 x 0.55 / 0.025^2 = 1521 hands

Worked hand (reading over-folding through the threshold): across 120 hands the opponent folded to a half-pot continuation bet 72 times, so FCB = 72 / 120 = 60.0%. The half-pot break-even fold rate is alpha = 4 / 12 = 33.3%, and 60.0% clears it by 26.7 points. Now add the noise: at p = 0.6 and n = 120 the half-width is about +/-8.8 points, so the lower bound is roughly 51% — still far above the threshold, which is what makes the adjustment evidence rather than a hunch.

Combinations beat single stats: wide opening plus a high fold rate to continuation bets means a wide, weakly defended range, so bet more often; narrow opening plus frequent re-raises means polarisation, so call less and fold more; three middling numbers mean there is nothing to harvest, so go back to baseline. A single stat only raises a hypothesis; the combination settles it.

Stats exist to eliminate hypotheses, not to confirm intuition: write down what you think he is, then see whether the numbers can overturn it. Keep the sample discipline too — a few dozen hands only fix the order of magnitude, hundreds are needed for percentage points, and every adjustment should answer 'how many hands does this conclusion need'.

Heads-up stat baselines and the sample they need: the baselines are empirical magnitudes, while the sample column is roughly how many hands it takes to read them — below that level a stat is a direction, not a conclusion.
t7hu-hand-reading: Hand Reading Is Shaving the Range Layer by Layer

Hand reading is not guessing two cards; it is deleting an impossible slice of combos at each decision point. Four steps: set the baseline range from preflop action; cut once by who the flop belongs to; cut again by the sizing on the turn; close it out with blockers on the river. Every step has to name the slice it removed — if you cannot name it, the range is still as wide as before and no reading happened.

Blocker combinatorics:

rank not on the board -> his pocket pair has C(4,2) = 6 combos
one of that rank on the board -> C(3,2) = 3 combos
one on the board plus one in your hand (two removed) -> C(2,2) = 1 combo

River board KS 9S 4D 7C 2S, you hold AS KD:
KK is down to 1 combo; 99 / 44 / 77 / 22 have 3 each (one of each rank on the board)
trips total 1 + 3 x 4 = 13 combos — value density shifts from trips-K to the small sets and two pair

Worked hand (blockers rewrite the call): on that river the opponent overbets 1.5x pot. The equilibrium bluff share at 1.5x is f = 1.5 / (1 + 2 x 1.5) = 37.5%, so value:bluff is about 5:3; if his value range holds 20 combos, equilibrium bluffs should be about 20 x 0.6 = 12. Your AS zeroes out his nut-flush combos, and KD cuts trips-K from 3 combos to 1 — the ace-high hand has no showdown value but is one of the best bluff-catchers available.

Worked hand (the narrowing ledger): about 600 combos open preflop; about 420 combos fire the KS 9S 4D flop; about 200 combos fire the 7C turn; about 60 combos are left to overbet the 2S river, of which 35 are value and 25 are bluffs.

bluff share 25 / 60 = 41.7%, above the 1.5x equilibrium of 37.5%
-> this opponent over-bluffs the river, so bluff-catching has positive margin
A Betting Line Is a Narrative

String the three streets together and they read as one sentence: small flop bet, turn check, big river bet reads as 'thin value on the flop, giving up the pressure on the turn, switching to a polarised size on the river' — not 'he was strong the whole way'. Half of hand reading is translating actions into a narrative.

Worked hand (checking the narrative against the sizing): 1/3 pot on the flop, check on the turn, 1.5x pot on the river. For that line to hang together the polarised river range has to be real: the equilibrium bluff share at 1.5x is 37.5%, so nearly four in ten of his river bets should be bluffs. A range that gave up the pressure on the turn and only then overbets the river usually cannot assemble that much value — when the narrative does not hold, bluff-catching has positive margin; and if you misread the turn check as a trap, the same line walks you into a wrong fold.

Counter-narrative first: when a line does not hang together — a turn check followed by a river overbet, for instance — suspect the narrative before you suspect your own reading. Inconsistency usually means you missed a node on one of the streets.

Four steps: set the baseline, cut by the board, cut by the sizing, close with blockers. And remember you are being read too — your own betting line has to fit your own range, or the opponent's counter-narrative lands first.
Range narrowing along one betting line (combo counts are a teaching setup): the value-to-bluff split on the river has to fit the sizing, otherwise the line is a counter-narrative.

t7hu-patterns-q1.question: The correct way to "read people" in heads-up is:
options: Inferring the opponent's range from frequencies (open rate / fold rate, etc.)
t7hu-patterns-q1.explanation: Reading is estimating ranges, not guessing hands. Cross the four key frequencies (open / fold / 3-bet / showdown) to infer the opponent's portrait.

t7hu-patterns-q2.question: An opponent opens 85% and folds to C-Bets 60%. The correct judgment is:
options: He's "wide range + weak defense" — C-Bet at high frequency to steal
t7hu-patterns-q2.explanation: Wide open + many folds = wide range with weak defense. C-Bet at high frequency as the last actor to steal, and widen your defense from the BB — harvest two leaks at once.

t7hu-patterns-q3.question: Against a calling station who almost never folds postflop, the correct exploitation is:
options: Value-bet thin value and reduce bluffs
t7hu-patterns-q3.explanation: A station doesn't fold, so pure bluffs are useless; switch to thin value bets because he calls with worse hands.

t7hu-patterns-q4.question: When identifying an opponent type, the sufficient sample size is about:
t7hu-patterns-q4.explanation: A single all-in win/loss is noise; only 50-100 hand frequency statistics form a reliable signal. Concluding from single-hand impressions is exploitation's biggest enemy.

t7hu-patterns-q5.question: An opponent opens only 30% and over-folds to raises (nit). The exploitation direction is:
t7hu-patterns-q5.explanation: A nit folds too much, so the fold rate on steals and raises is automatic profit. But note he's usually strong once in a pot — avoid being re-raised by his occasional strong hands.

t7hu-patterns-q6.question: The opponent folds to a half-pot continuation bet 72 times in 120 hands. What is the FCB and how does it compare with the half-pot threshold?
options: 60.0%, above the 33.3% threshold, so bet more often
t7hu-patterns-q6.explanation: 72 / 120 = 60.0%; the half-pot break-even fold rate is alpha = 4 / 12 = 33.3%, so 60.0% clears it by 26.7 points.

t7hu-patterns-q7.question: The opponent opens wide but rarely re-raises. The combined read is:
options: Wide and passive: bluff less, thin-value more
Wide and aggressive: play only the nuts
t7hu-patterns-q7.explanation: A wide range with few re-raises means plenty of weak calling hands: bluffs get called, thin value gets paid.

t7hu-patterns-q8.question: The opponent shows down the nuts in an all-in. The right response is:
options: Keep the profile and wait for frequency evidence across 50-100 hands
Classify him as a nit immediately
Give him more respect and stop betting
t7hu-patterns-q8.explanation: One hand is noise: profiles come from frequencies, not single showdowns, and changing one takes a sample rather than an impression.

t7hu-exploit-q1.question: The discipline of "minimum necessary deviation" is:
options: Aiming at the opponent's leak with minimal magnitude, ready to return to baseline anytime
t7hu-exploit-q1.explanation: Deviations open your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled; aim at the leak, keep it minimal, and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

t7hu-exploit-q2.question: Against an opponent with a 60% fold rate (equilibrium 40%), the steal EV is:
t7hu-exploit-q2.explanation: EV = 0.6×1.5 − 0.4×1.5 = +0.3BB, pure stealing already profits. The higher the opponent's fold rate, the more your steal frequency should rise.

t7hu-exploit-q3.question: The purpose of node locking is:
options: Locking your own strategy to prevent misclicks
Fixing the opponent's strategy to the observed tendency and solving the maximally exploitative response
t7hu-exploit-q3.explanation: Node locking feeds "how the opponent actually plays" into the solver and outputs the optimal harvest scheme for that deviation — turning exploitation from feel into calculation.

t7hu-exploit-q4.question: Against a station who calls too loosely postflop, the exploitation adjustment is:
options: Increase value bets and put thin-value hands into the betting range
t7hu-exploit-q4.explanation: The station calls with weak hands, so your wide value range gets overpaid — increase value-bet sizes and include thin-value hands in the betting range.

t7hu-exploit-q5.question: After you raise steal frequency, the opponent starts 3-betting frequently. The correct move is:
options: Return to the GTO baseline and narrow the range
t7hu-exploit-q5.explanation: The opponent detected your deviation, and your newly opened leaks will be harvested in reverse. You must return to baseline — exploitation is a "deviate → get detected → return" dynamic game.

t7hu-exploit-q6.question: Steal-raising to 2BB (with the 0.5 dead small blind already sunk), the opponent folds 45%. The expectation is:
t7hu-exploit-q6.explanation: EV = 0.45 x 1.5 - 0.55 x 1.5 = 0.675 - 0.825 = -0.15BB; the break-even fold rate is 50%.

t7hu-exploit-q7.question: What should cap the size of an exploitative adjustment?
options: You are still not losing if the opponent corrects back to around the break-even line
t7hu-exploit-q7.explanation: Every deviation opens a hole of your own: cap it at the point where you still do not lose once he corrects, because anything beyond that gets harvested in reverse.

t7hu-exploit-q8.question: With a 70% fold rate, the expectation of a steal is:

t7hu-stats-q1.question: VPIP is defined as:
options: Hands with voluntary money in divided by total hands
Preflop raises divided by total hands
Pots won divided by total hands
t7hu-stats-q1.explanation: VPIP counts voluntary money only (calls and raises); the forced big blind is not included, and PFR is a subset of it.

t7hu-stats-q2.question: 35 VPIP hands out of 150. What is the VPIP?
t7hu-stats-q2.explanation: 35 / 150 = 23.3%; with 28 preflop raises the PFR is 28 / 150 = 18.7%, a gap of 4.6 points.

t7hu-stats-q3.question: 60 bets, 30 raises and 30 calls. What is the aggression factor?
t7hu-stats-q3.explanation: AF = (60 + 30) / 30 = 3.0; with zero calls AF is undefined and you have to fall back to the raw counts.

t7hu-stats-q4.question: Why can PFR never exceed VPIP?
options: A preflop raise is a subset of putting voluntary money in
t7hu-stats-q4.explanation: Every preflop raise is also money voluntarily in the pot, so PFR never exceeds VPIP; the gap is exactly the hands played without raising.

t7hu-stats-q5.question: With n = 100 and p = 0.45, the 95% interval half-width is about:
t7hu-stats-q5.explanation: SE = sqrt(0.45 x 0.55 / 100) = 5.0 points, so the half-width is 1.96 x SE = 9.8 points.

t7hu-stats-q6.question: To pull the half-width down to 2.5 points (p = 0.45), you need about:
t7hu-stats-q6.explanation: n >= 1.96^2 x 0.45 x 0.55 / 0.025^2 = 1521; the half-width scales as 1/sqrt(n), so halving it takes four times the sample.

t7hu-stats-q7.question: A high open rate plus a high fold rate to continuation bets reads as, and calls for:
options: A wide, weakly defended range: bet and steal more often
A calling station: value bet only
No leak: go back to baseline
t7hu-stats-q7.explanation: Wide but willing to fold is the softest fold equity available; still keep a hand free for his occasional strong holding instead of escalating a steal into a war.

t7hu-stats-q8.question: Which statement about reading heads-up stats is correct?
options: A single stat only raises a hypothesis; a sample and a combination settle it
One stat is enough to pin the opponent's type
The smaller the sample the better
Stats tell you the opponent's exact hand
t7hu-stats-q8.explanation: Stats describe the shape of a range, not two specific cards; hundreds of hands and two or three cross-checks are what support an adjustment.

t7hu-hand-reading-q1.question: The correct order of the four reading steps is:
options: Baseline preflop, cut by board, cut by sizing, close with blockers
t7hu-hand-reading-q1.explanation: Ranges are shaved from wide to narrow street by street: the baseline is widest, board and sizing each cut once, and blockers close it.

t7hu-hand-reading-q2.question: River board KS 9S 4D 7C 2S, you hold AS KD. How many combos of KK can the opponent hold?
t7hu-hand-reading-q2.explanation: KS on the board and KD in your hand remove two kings, leaving two, so C(2,2) = 1; with one on the board it is C(3,2) = 3, and with none 6.

t7hu-hand-reading-q3.question: One 9 is on the board and you hold none. How many combos of 99 can the opponent hold?
t7hu-hand-reading-q3.explanation: C(3,2) = 3: one nine is on the board, so two are drawn from the remaining three.

t7hu-hand-reading-q4.question: The equilibrium bluff share of a 1.5x pot bet is:
t7hu-hand-reading-q4.explanation: f = b/(1+2b) = 1.5 / 4 = 37.5%, so value:bluff is about 5:3. 33.3% is full pot and 28.6% is 2/3 pot.

t7hu-hand-reading-q5.question: The opponent's 1.5x river value range holds 20 combos. At equilibrium, how many bluffs should there be?

t7hu-hand-reading-q6.question: A line of small flop bet, turn check, big river bet usually reads as:
options: Thin value on the flop, pressure abandoned on the turn, a polarised size on the river
A probe on the flop and pot control on the river
t7hu-hand-reading-q6.explanation: The actions form a narrative: small thin value, no turn pressure, then a polarised river — not strength from start to finish.

t7hu-hand-reading-q7.question: When a betting line does not hang together, the right priority is:
options: Suspect the narrative first, your own reading second
t7hu-hand-reading-q7.explanation: Inconsistency usually means a missed node on one street; fix the narrative model before deciding to call or fold.

t7hu-hand-reading-q8.question: Why must your own betting line stay consistent with your range?
options: Otherwise the opponent's counter-narrative lands first and your line becomes free information
t7hu-hand-reading-q8.explanation: You are being read too: when your line contradicts your range the opponent can price against the contradiction, and both your bluffs and your value get handled cheaply.
